youtube_description:
⚡ The chart-race that explains why the global grid started betting against coal.

In this video, we animate a high-contrast timeline of electricity generation shares from 2000 → 2026, tracking the solar boom vs coal bust—plus the “buffer” roles of natural gas and nuclear.

00:00 — The baseline: coal still dominates, solar barely shows up (2000)
02:10 — Early signals: cost declines start bending the curve (2004–2008)
04:05 — The inflection: utility solar scales fast enough to matter (2010–2013)
06:20 — Policy + deployment snowball: coal’s share starts sliding (2014–2017)
08:40 — The big squeeze: 2018–2020 shows the momentum, not just the trend
10:55 — Post-pandemic energy remix: gas helps short-term, renewables keep climbing (2021–2022)
12:30 — The coal bust era: retirements + demand shifts push share down (2023–2026)

By the end, watch the moment when renewables cross a “tipping” threshold while coal continues losing ground—turning the grid into a solar-and-wind-led system.

instagram_caption:
🚀 Coal didn’t “die” overnight—its share bled out while solar-and-wind quietly scaled into a new grid.

Here’s the dramatic timeline: in 2000, coal powered about 38.6% of the world’s electricity. Meanwhile, the solar-and-wind stack was practically a rounding error at roughly 0.9%. For years, the story looked like a slow grind—coal flat, renewables growing, but not fast enough to reshape dispatch.

Then the inflection hit. From 2004 to 2010, solar-and-wind climbed from ~1.4% to ~3.2%, and the curve kept steepening. By 2013, renewables were up near ~4.8%, while coal drifted down to ~35.0%. This is where the “market math” changes: each new GW of clean capacity doesn’t just add power—it also displaces the next increment of generation planning.

The mid-2010s are where it gets brutal. By 2015, coal had fallen to ~34.3% while solar-and-wind reached ~6.4%. Through 2018–2019, renewables kept accelerating (to ~9.1% and ~10.2%), and coal’s share kept sliding (down to ~33.1% and ~32.7%). Natural gas rises too—acting like the short-term stabilizer—while nuclear barely moves.

Fast forward to the “coal bust era.” In 2022 coal drops further to ~31.9%, and by 2026 it’s projected around ~29.0%. In the same span, solar-and-wind rises to ~18.4%. The visual payoff is the moment renewables clearly stop being the side story.

💬 Question for you: In your country, do you think renewables will keep outpacing coal primarily due to (1) policy, (2) economics/costs, or (3) grid integration speed?

facebook_caption:
Coal’s global electricity share declined steadily while solar-and-wind surged—creating a clear, data-driven transition in power markets. In 2000, coal accounted for about 38.6% of global electricity generation; by 2026, that share is shown at roughly 29.0%. Over the same period, combined solar and wind generation share grows from about 0.9% to approximately 18.4%, crossing multiple “momentum” thresholds in the 2010s and 2020s.

Natural gas rises during the transition, reflecting its role as a flexible backup, while nuclear remains comparatively stable. The timeline illustrates a high-contrast shift: coal loses share through retirements, demand changes, and new build momentum, while renewables scale into a dominant planning assumption.
